extracted.intended_audience: researchers and designers of news recommender systems (academics and practitioners)
extracted.subtask_short: news recommender system design and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for designing, implementing, and evaluating news recommender systems (NRS), with emphasis on accuracy, beyond-accuracy aspects (diversity, serendipity, novelty), user experience, privacy, and societal impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (standard evaluation measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is considered as a standard evaluation measure to assess the quality of a recommender system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important but insufficient alone; should be combined with beyond-accuracy aspects (diversity, novelty, serendipity) because accuracy-centric designs can produce negative effects (filter bubbles, boredom). Often evaluated offline but online evaluation is preferable when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversification in an NRS is necessary not only to keep readers engaged in the reading process, but also to keep readers from becoming trapped in filter bubbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be introduced via regularization (e.g., balancing Ridge for accuracy and Lasso for diversity), re-ranking, multi-arm bandit with exploration–exploitation tradeoff, neural attention adjustments, or aspect-level presentation. Must be balanced with accuracy to avoid totally arbitrary recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage is a beyond-accuracy aspect that contributes to the quality of news recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-offs exist between coverage and accuracy; consider coverage metrics when designing algorithms (e.g., budgeted maximum coverage) and in evaluation protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is an important beyond-accuracy criterion for news recommendation quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should be measured alongside accuracy and diversity to enhance user experience; novelty metrics may conflict with personalization and popularity signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serendipity
rubrics_metrics.description: Serendipity is a beyond-accuracy measure important for user experience in NRS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade-offs such as accuracy-serendipity and diversity-serendipity (e.g., Maksai et al. quantify such trade-offs). Use dedicated metrics and user studies when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization (degree of personalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization is often the result of recommendations that align highly with users’ preferences. Usually, a high accuracy results in higher personalization in a recommender system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should not be maximized blindly—over-personalization can create filter bubbles and boredom. Aim to balance personalization with reasonable diversity and allow user control where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective exposure / presenting multiple perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective exposure is presented as a solution to counteract filter bubbles by exposing users to differing viewpoints and perspectives on news topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify or cluster news articles by aspects (styles, tags, categories, sentiments) and provide different perspectives; combine with nudges and interface design to encourage exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudge theory (ethical nudging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nudge theory: giving subtle nudge (touch or push) in the form of small design changes that encourage users to make other choices in their general interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used transparently and ethically, nudges can guide users toward politically balanced consumption or greater engagement; be wary of manipulative or opaque nudging (real-world examples show risk of steering toward sensational or fake news). Consider designs like Resnick et al.'s browser add-on and documented 'smart nudge' architectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs among evaluation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are trade-offs between different metrics such as accuracy-coverage, accuracy-diversity, accuracy-serendipity, diversity-serendipity to test recommendation performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify and analyze these trade-offs (Maksai et al.); design optimization or regularization approaches to balance conflicting objectives and report multiple metrics in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency / Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness and recency are prominent challenges in NRS due to dynamically generated news and evolving reader preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recency as an explicit factor (e.g., recency-relevance trade-offs), and use stream-based or session-based models to capture time-sensitive interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / Popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance (or popularity) of news stories is a key factor that should be balanced with recency and diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine popularity signals with personalization (e.g., Chakraborty et al.'s recency-importance-diversity balance or the proposed future-impact metric) to predict impact for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-impact metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed metric that takes the popularity signals from crowd-sourced information and the personalized information from past news data to predict the impact of news stories for a news reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a way to balance recency, popularity and personalization when selecting stories likely to be impactful for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Trustworthiness: level of user trust on the system is an important evaluation aspect for NRS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider credibility detection, provenance, and explanations; align recommendation behavior with norms that build user trust (transparency, privacy safeguards, anti-manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and regulatory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving privacy and complying with regulations (e.g., GDPR) are requirements for recommender systems that affect trust and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design privacy-preserving mechanisms (data minimization, opt-outs, anonymization) and ensure profiling and data use comply with legal/regulatory frameworks to avoid misuse of personal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency (computational/interaction efficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency: ease of the search and accessibility of the information is an evaluation aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider real-time constraints and computational cost; optimize models for latency and resource usage (quantization, compression, pruning) to enable online evaluation and deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Robustness: ability to make relevant predictions in the presence of noisy data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate under noisy or adversarial conditions; design algorithms resilient to manipulation (e.g., social media manipulation, fake news propagation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability and Explainability
rubrics_metrics.description: DL methods behave like blackboxes, providing limited interpretability and little explainability in recommendation tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop interpretable models or explanation modules (e.g., attention visualizations, feature attributions) so designers and users can understand why recommendations are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation protocols: offline vs online
rubrics_metrics.description: Offline evaluation is the most popular model evaluation protocol, though online evaluations and user studies are used too but are costly for large-scale news data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, complement offline evaluation with online tests or realistic streaming benchmarks (CLEF NEWSREEL, MIND); reduce computational costs to enable real-time experiments or use simulation/living-lab setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: User experience benchmarking / need for NRS-specific UX framework
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no benchmark to evaluate user experiences in a recommender system specific to news; existing frameworks are expensive and rely on user studies only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a benchmark user modeling framework tailored to NRS that integrates accuracy and beyond-accuracy aspects and is feasible under real-time constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset availability and benchmarking platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: There are very few (often private) datasets in NRS; more challenges (e.g., CLEF NEWSREEL, MIND Leaderboard) are needed to encourage real-time research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage open datasets, leaderboards, and standard benchmarks to facilitate reproducible research and realistic evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit user feedback interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit ratings are used to infer latent information but it can be tricky to decide whether implicit feedback is positive or negative (e.g., time spent might be idle; skips may indicate boredom or repetition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully design signals and features to distinguish positive vs. negative engagement; consider multi-signal approaches and validate with user studies when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gamification for engagement and cold-start
rubrics_metrics.description: Gamification: use of game design elements (points, badges, avatars, leaderboards) to motivate and promote user activities; not widely used in NRS but potentially useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gamification to improve engagement and overcome cold-start but design ethically to avoid manipulation and ensure alignment with news-reading goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating manipulative effects (fake news, echo chambers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing solutions (selective exposure, diversity-aware algorithms, banning manipulative practices) are insufficient; systems need ways to prevent, detect and break down effects like filter bubbles and echo chambers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop algorithmic or heuristic detection mechanisms for manipulation and fake news; test at scale (beyond small experiments); combine detection with transparency and content provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect-level presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect is a collection of attributes, components, or services used to categorize information; aspect-level presentation can diversify recommendations by providing different perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify or cluster news by aspects (topics, styles, tags, sentiments) and surface multiple aspects to the user to increase exposure diversity; research in aspect-level presentation is limited but promising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer learning suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer learning can address data sparsity by transferring knowledge from large pre-trained models, but the pre-trained model should be based on the news dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid transferring noise/outliers from unrelated domains; when using pre-trained models, prefer ones trained or fine-tuned on news-like corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and computational resource considerations for DL models
rubrics_metrics.description: DL methods demand much more data and parameter tuning and behave like blackboxes; they also require more computational resources than standard methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use model compression, pruning, quantization, or efficient architectures (e.g., Reformer) to reduce cost; account for latency and resource constraints in real-time NRS deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity through neural attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Neural attention can be used to introduce diversity in session-based recommenders; attention mechanisms may overweight repeated clicks leading to similar recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dampen importance of repeated clicks (assign scaling weights to query vectors) and give weight to non-repeated actions to increase diversity; little work so far—opportunity for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing user control and transparency in recommendation design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design algorithms so users can indicate their interests and receive relevant (novel, recent, important) content from diversified sources; transparency should give a clearer view of the world rather than an echo chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide interfaces and controls (filters, toggles, explanation of signals) that let users shape recommendations; couple with transparent descriptions of data use and algorithmic behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary research imperative
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for interdisciplinary research combining social science and computer science expertise to address challenges specific to the news domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborate across disciplines to design evaluation metrics that capture societal impact (democratic role, ideological segregation) and to develop detection/mitigation strategies for social harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving democratic / civic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: NRS should play a democratic, liberal and deliberative role in the community rather than merely maximizing engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recommendations to reduce ideological segregation, avoid manipulative practices, increase exposure diversity, and support civic information needs; include societal-impact metrics in evaluations.
